title: Departments Paying Above the Average
description: Compare each department's average salary with the average of the whole company, using a subquery in HAVING.
statement:
Return each department whose **average salary is higher than the average salary of all employees** in the company (including the people who belong to no department). Columns: `department` and `avg_salary`, the department's average rounded to a whole number.

Highest first.
starter:
SELECT name AS department
FROM departments;
hints: You need two averages in one query. One is per department; what makes the other one different?
`GROUP BY` the department, `HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)`.
The subquery must look at all employees, including those with no department.
solution:
SELECT d.name AS department, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_salary
FROM departments AS d
JOIN employees AS e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
HAVING AVG(e.salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC, department;
explanation:
**The idea.** Two different averages: one per group (the `AVG` in `HAVING`), one for the whole table (a scalar subquery `(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)`, which runs once and returns a single number). `HAVING` compares them, keeping the groups above the company figure.

**Why the subquery looks at `employees` and not at the joined rows.** The company average must include employees with no department; the joined rows (inner join with departments) would leave them out and change the number.

**Usual mistakes.** Comparing to the average of the department averages (a different number when departments differ in size); writing the subquery condition in `WHERE`; rounding before comparing.
